title: Improving Code Localization with Repository Memory
claim: A memory built from past history is exposed to an agent through a small set of retrieval tools used during its reasoning.
layout: 2 panels, memory left, tools center, agent trace right, bidirectional arrows
description: A diagram with an issue description box at top center, in blue, showing a NameError bug report. Arrows lead from it down-left and down-right. The left column, panel (a) 'Constructing Repository Memory', has two gray boxes. 'Recent history commits' lists commit hashes, messages and file paths. A down arrow leads to 'Summary of actively evolving files', which gives per-file functionality summaries. Key terms are highlighted in red and orange. The center is a peach 'Tooling' box with four buttons: SearchCommit, ExamineCommit, ViewSummary and SearchSummary, plus '(+ existing tools)'. Double-headed blue arrows connect the tools to both the memory boxes and the right column. The right column, panel (b) 'Integration with Agentic Frameworks', shows a robot icon and an agent trace. The trace alternates Thought, Action and Observation steps and ends in 'Localization'.
caption: An overview of our repository memory design. (a) We construct the memory by leveraging the recent commit history of the repository. This involves creating a searchable database of past commits and their linked issues, and identifying frequently edited files to let LLMs generate high-level functionality summaries. (b) The memory is accessed by the language agent via a set of tools that perform search based on custom queries and support closer examination of individual memory entries. Details in \S[ref].
abstract: Code localization is a fundamental challenge in repository-level software engineering tasks such as bug fixing. While existing methods equip language agents with comprehensive tools/interfaces to fetch information from the repository, they overlook the critical aspect of memory, where each instance is typically handled from scratch assuming no prior repository knowledge. In contrast, human developers naturally build long-term repository memory, such as the functionality of key modules and associations between various bug types and their likely fix locations. In this work, we augment language agents with such memory by leveraging a repository's commit history -- a rich yet underutilized resource that chronicles the codebase's evolution. We introduce tools that allow the agent to retrieve from a non-parametric memory encompassing recent historical commits and linked issues, as well as functionality summaries of actively evolving parts of the codebase identified via commit patterns. We demonstrate that augmenting such a memory can significantly improve LocAgent, a state-of-the-art localization framework, on both SWE-bench-verified and the more recent SWE-bench-live benchmarks. Our research contributes towards developing agents that can accumulate and leverage past experience for long-horizon tasks, more closely emulating the expertise of human developers.
